O R D E R
1. Delay in filing/refiling is condoned.
2. Permission to file Miscellaneous Applications/Contempt
Petition(s) is granted.
3

## Page 20

3. Applications  for  substitution  are  allowed  after
condoning the delay and setting aside the abatement. Cause
title be amended accordingly.
Contempt Petition(C) Diary No.75518/2025 (It.46.45)
4. At this stage, we are informed that despite judgment
dated  10.07.2024  passed  in  C.A.  Nos.3674-3675/2023,  the
enhanced compensation has not been paid to the successful
landowners.
5. In the interest of justice, we grant three months’ more
time to NOIDA to do the needful, failing which there will be
punitive  action  against  the  responsible
officers/authorities.
6. The Contempt Petition(s) is, accordingly, disposed of.
Rest of the matters
7. These Miscellaneous Applications have been moved by
landowners whom the High Court had granted compensation at
the rate of Rs.340 per sq. yd. Moreover, these a pplicants
are those who did not approach this Court for further
enhancement originally.
8. However, the similarly placed landowners, whose lands
were also acquired in the same village through the same
acquisition process, approached this Court through a batch
of  appeals,  which  were  allowed  vide judgment  dated
4

## Page 21

10.07.2024 and compensation was enhanced from Rs.340 per sq.
yd. to Rs.403 per sq. yd.
9. Pursuant thereto, the instant applicants have also filed
these  Miscellaneous  Applications  on  06.09.2024,  seeking
parity in the matter of grant of higher compensation.
10. Shri Ravinder Kumar, learned Senior Counsel for NOIDA,
has vehemently opposed these prayers, as according to him,
neither the Miscellaneous Applications are maintainable nor
the applicants, who had earlier accepted the rate of Rs.340
per sq. yd., can be permitted to turn around and seek a
higher compensation at this belated stage.
11. Upon consideration of the rival submissions, we are
satisfied that the applicants are entitled to seek parity
with the similarly placed landowners, primarily on the anvil
of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and claim the
same rate of compensation. However, the principles of equity
can be balanced by directing that the applicants shall not
be entitled to any interest for the delayed period.
12. Consequently, the Miscellaneous Applications are allowed
and the applicants are also held entitled to compensation at
the rate of Rs.403 per sq. yd.; however, the statutory
interest on such enhanced compensation shall be admissible
to them only from the date they approached this Court by way
of the appropriate applications.
13. NOIDA is directed to calculate and pay the enhanced
5

## Page 22

compensation to the applicants within a period of three
months.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
Transfer Petition (C) No.3413 of 2024
Romani Bansal
…. Petitioner
Versus
Abhishek Kumar                 …. Respondent
O R D E R 
The transfer petition by the wife essentially seeks transfer of
the petition filed by the husband under Section 9 of the Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955  from Ranchi to Himachal Pradesh, wherein the
wife is residing with her mother and two children. The petitioner is a
Pediatrician and the respondent is a Physician. Considering the best
interest of the children and also considering the fact that the
petitioner and the respondent are medical professionals, we wanted
to interact with them, especially since earlier attempts at mediation
failed. By our last order, we directed the petitioner and the
respondent to be present, with the children.
2. Today, we took up the matter in the Committee Room. Of the
two children, we were informed that the first one is undergoing
1 of 5

## Page 32

coaching for his higher studies in Chandigarh and was unable to
come to Delhi. However, the petitioner, respondent and their
daughter were present. We interacted with the petitioner, her
daughter and the husband separately. We also heard learned
Counsel who were appearing for the respective parties.
3. Without disclosing the details, suffice it to observe that we
were convinced that the marriage has irretrievably broken down.
However, it is also a fact that the respondent is visiting the children
regularly at their mother’s residence in Himachal Pradesh. The
petitioner-wife also does not have any objection in the same being
continued. The petitioner does not seek anything for herself in the
nature of alimony. She also submits that she will look after the
children.
4. Again, considering the best interest of the children, we were of
the opinion that the respondent should support the petitioner at
least to the extent of the needs of the children. The respondent also
submitted before us that he has been giving Rs.50,000/- to the
petitioner for their children, which is denied by the petitioner
alleging that the amounts given were sporadic and not continuous.
In any event the statement made by the respondent indicates his
2 of 5

## Page 33

inclination to support the children. We are hence of the opinion that
the respondent should deposit an amount of Rs.1,00,000/- every
month into the account of the petitioner for the requirements of the
children. We make it clear that this does not mean that the
respondent should not otherwise support the children in their
studies, in future and financially support them at the time of
marriage.
5. The petitioner is also not averse to the visitation rights as
claimed by the respondent, which according to her, he has been
utilizing every month, by visiting the children at Himachal Pradesh.
The visitation rights will be continued and the respondent permitted
to meet the children on a monthly basis either at Himachal Pradesh
or at the place where the children are housed for their studies; the
son being now at Chandigarh.
6. There was a request made by the learned Counsel for the
respondent for interim custody during vacation, so that the
grandparents can meet the children. However, this has to be subject
to the convenience of the children and also their desire. There would
be no impediment to the grandparents meeting the children either
at Himachal Pradesh or, as observed above, at the place where they
3 of 5

## Page 34

are housed for their studies. Just as the visitation rights, we leave it
to the parties to come to a meeting point especially looking at the
convenience of the children and their desire. It would be better that
we do not make any concrete directions to that end.
7. In the above circumstances, we dispose of the petition between
the  parties,  invoking  our  powers  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India and dissolving the marriage finding it to have
irretrievably broken down. The following directions are passed in
disposal of the above petition.
a. The marriage between the petitioner and the respondent
solemnized on 13.10.2008 stands dissolved.
b. The respondent shall remit an amount of Rs.1,00,000/- to
the account of the petitioner on every month before the
10th of that month till the children attain majority, the
amount being utilized equally for the welfare of the two
children.
c. Insofar as the visitation rights of the father and the
grandparents, since the parties are in cordial terms and
have been carrying permitting such visitation, we are of the
4 of 5

## Page 35

opinion that parties should be left to decide the terms.
8. Noticing the fact that there are pending proceedings between
the parties, we make it clear that all of those; both civil or criminal,
arising from the marriage and discord therefrom, will be terminated
on this order.
9. The parties shall not raise any further claims with respect to
the marriage, hereafter.
10. The transfer petition shall stand disposed of. 
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
.……………………………... J.
                                                (J. B. PARDIWALA)
..………….…………………. J.
                                                           (K. VINOD CHANDRAN)
NEW DELHI;
AUGUST 13, 2026.

1. This special leave petition questions the compensation awarded
for acquisition of the land.

a settlement.

Secretary, District Legal Services Authority, Koppal.

deed dated 14.08.2026. Paragraph 2 of the settlement which is
relevant reads as under:

## Page 44

“2. The terms of settlement are as under:
a) That the claimant(s) Appellant(s) and
Respondents agreed to compromise in the
above  case,  the  appellant  is  entitled
market  value  of  Rs.3,80,000/-  per  acre
along with other statutory benefits
b) Both parties admits the double market
value of the land acquired as per the first
schedule to the Right to Fair Compensation
and  Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013.
c) 100% market value of acquired land under
section  30(1)  of  the  Right  to  Fair
Compensation  and  Transparency  in  Land
Acquisition,  Rehabilitation  and
Resettlement Act 2013.
d)  The  claimants  shall  receive  12%
additional value under section 30(3) of the
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency
in  Land  Acquisition,  Rehabilitation  and
Resettlement Act 2013.
e)  The  claimants  shall  entitle  to  9%
interest per annum for the first year,
calculated from the date of the Section
4(1) notification under section of 80 of
the  Right  to  Fair  Compensation  and
Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013.
f) The claimants admits to waived the right
to this 15% interest for a period of 2
financial years only. The rider is state
shall deposit the amount within 3 months
from the date of settlement.
g) Both parties agree that these terms
completely settle all claims and disputes
regarding this land acquisition. No further
claims can be made.
h)  The  claimants  agrees  that  any
compensation amount already paid by the
state will be deducted from this final
settled amount.
i) Any compensation already paid will be
deducted, and the state shall deposit the

## Page 45

remaining balance into the court within 3
months  from  the  date  of  the  order.
j) Both parties agree that once the court
closes this matter based on this Joint
Memo, neither side will file any appeal,
review, or Special Leave Petition (SLP) in
any higher court. This settlement is final
and binding on both parties.
k) The parties agree that the above terms
constitute a full and final settlement of
all claims and disputes arising out of the
present land acquisition proceedings.”    
5. The parties who have appeared through video conferencing from 
the office of DLSA, Koppal have affirmed the settlement.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Amicus Curiae and the
learned Senior counsel/counsel appearing for the
parties.
2. We have taken note of the issues flagged by the
learned  Amicus,  with  specific  reference  to  the
States of Punjab and Maharashtra on their non-
compliance with the directions and suggestions made
by the Committee for “Ensuring the implementation of
the Decisions of the Apex Court.”
3. Learned counsel appearing for the aforesaid two
States submit that due compliance will be made and
reported to the learned Amicus shortly.

## Page 63

9
4. We have also taken note of the fact that the
meetings of the District Level Empowered Committees
(DLECs) are not being regularly held, as mandated in
the revised SOP dated 02.12.2025. Hence, it is
directed that all the DLECs shall meet regularly, as
mandated, and also take decisions on the cases that
are  pending  consideration  before  them.  The
compliance of the above must be made and reported to
the learned Amicus before the next date of hearing.
5. We further take note of the fact that in some
cases, the DLECs have kept cases pending without any
decision,  despite  several  meetings  having  taken
place. Data submitted by the State of Uttar Pradesh
reflects  that  many  cases  are  still  pending
consideration  before  the  DLEC  with  no  decision
having been taken. Hence, it is directed that all
the States must ensure that the concerned DLECs are
taking timely decisions on the cases that come
before them for consideration, instead of deferring
and adjourning the same. The compliance of the above
must be made and reported to the learned Amicus
before the next date of hearing.
6. We have been apprised by the learned Amicus that
in some cases in the State of Uttar Pradesh, the
Financial/Social  Status  Reports  of  Under  Trial
Prisoners  (UTPs)  are  still  awaited  from  the
respective District Legal Services Authority (DLSA),

## Page 64

10
due to which cases have remained pending for months
without  possible  consideration  by  the  Empowered
Committee. Hence, the NALSA is directed to ensure
that all DLSAs ensure that adequate steps are taken
so that cases do not remain pending for want of
Financial/Social Status Reports.  The compliance of
the above must be made and reported to the learned
Amicus before the next date of hearing.
7. We have heard the learned Solicitor General and
Mr. Prashant Bhushan, learned AOR, appearing for the
applicant in IA No.79978/2026.
8. The matters stand adjourned by four weeks to
await  the  report  on  the  main  issues  and  also
suggestions on IA No.79978/2026.
9. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  Contempt
Petitioner in Contempt Petition [C] No.348/2026 is
permitted to serve papers on the learned Amicus
Curiae, in the meantime.
10. List the matter on 06.10.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These petitions, at the instance of the homebuyers, seek a
direction  to  respondent  no.6  -  M/s  Mahira  Buildtech  Private
Limited, as well as to the authorities of the State of Haryana, to
complete the various planned housing projects under the affordable
housing policy of the State of Haryana.
2. To  explicate,  the  Mahira  Homes  projects  comprise  5292
residential units in five projects, comprising 42 residential
towers. It is a matter of record that the projects were to commence
in the year 2017-2018 and the builder was obligated to complete and
hand over possession by the end of 2021. It is also undeniable that
while the project in Sector 68 is completed up to 75%, that in
Sector 103 is completed only up to 15%. The petitioner-homebuyers
have alleged that the entire amount of allotment price has been
taken from them, and the respondent-builder has siphoned away these
monies, leaving the projects incomplete. 
3. At this stage, the issue with which we are primarily concerned
is  to  explore  the  modalities  for  completion  of  the  pending
projects. The homebuyers have suggested that an entity under the
Government of India, such as the NBCC, may be entrusted to take
over the projects and complete the same. 
4. Learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties are agreeable
that a fair enhancement in the allotment price may be effected so
that a corpus of funds can be created for an entity like NBCC or
any other builder-cum-developer, who might be inclined to complete
5

## Page 92

the pending projects under the supervision of a Committee that may
be constituted by this Court. 
5. We, therefore, request Ms. Rajiv Jain, learned Amicus Curiae ,
to contact NBCC or any other Government undertaking, which is
willing to complete the pending projects. Let the terms and
conditions on which the proposal would be acceptable to them also
be ascertained, so that the agreement of the homebuyers can also be
sought.
6. Learned  Amicus  may also consider the material on record,
including  the  reports  said  to  have  been  submitted  by  the
Enforcement Directorate, to identify the unencumbered assets of the
defaulting builder. The appropriate directions in that regard will
be issued after a report on the same is submitted by the learned
Amicus. 
7. Meanwhile, learned counsel for the homebuyers will also have
instructions regarding the above proposal. Since the Affordable
Housing Policy has been evolved by the State of Haryana and the
rate  of  allotment  of  such  scheme  is  implemented  under  the
supervision of the State Authorities, we direct the State of
Haryana also to explore as to whether the pending project can be
completed by a State Agency like the Housing Board Haryana or
Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP).
8. Unfortunately, no one has entered appearance on behalf of the
State today. The Registry is directed to inform the Standing
Counsel of this order, who shall have instructions and remain
present in Court on the next date of hearing.
9. Meanwhile, we also deem it appropriate to direct the District
6

## Page 93

Town  and  Country  Planning,  Gurugram  (DTCP),  to  prepare  an
exhaustive statement of the entire inventory regarding all the
projects, including the allotments made as well as the inventory
available for allotment, and submit a comprehensive report before
this Court. For that, the DTCP is permitted to summon the builder’s
record. This report shall also be furnished to the learned Amicus
to enable him to place the accurate state of affairs before the
NBCC/other entity(s).
10. Meanwhile, there shall be a stay on any further allotments of
units in the subject projects.
11. Post the matters on 13.10.2026.

Babalal H1; Raj Reddy Kallem v. State of Haryana2; B. V. Seshaiah v.

N.I. Act is compoundable with the consent of the parties at any
stage, even after conviction.  These Special Leave Petition(s) are

punishable under Section 138 of the N.I. Act are hereby compounded.

aside.

PARAMJIT KAUR                                     APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB & ANR.                          RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This  appeal  challenges  the  order  dated
05.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M No.1363 of 2026.
Apprehending arrest in connection with crime
registered pursuant to FIR No. 140 of 2025 lodged
with P.S. I.T. City, District SAS Nagar in respect
of the offences punishable under Sections 80, 61(2)
and 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (“BNS”
for short), the appellant preferred an application
before the High Court seeking anticipatory bail in
terms of Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023(“BNSS” for short).
1

## Page 137

The application for anticipatory bail having
been rejected by the High Court vide the impugned
order dated 05.02.2026, the instant appeal has been
preferred.
By order dated 10.03.2026, this Court passed
the following order: 
“Issue  notice  to  the  respondent,
returnable on 24.04.2026. 
Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-
State accepts notice. 
No coercive steps shall be taken as
against the petitioner herein vis-a-vis FIR
No.140 of 2025 dated 10.10.2025, PS IT
City, District SAS Nagar, subject to the
petitioner  cooperating  with  the
investigation of the case.”
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
in support of the appeal and learned counsel for
the respondent(s)-State and perused the material on
record.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that
the appellant has cooperated with the investigation and
her  husband  has  also  been  granted  the  relief  of
anticipatory bail. Hence, on the principle of parity,
the appellant also may be granted the same relief by
setting aside the impugned order and further by making
2

## Page 138

interim order absolute.
By way of response, learned counsel for the
respondent(s)-State  submitted  that  the
investigation will be completed and most probably
the charge sheet even against the appellant herein
may  be  filed  shortly.  In  the  circumstances,
appropriate orders may be made.
Considering the circumstances on record, in our
view, the appellant is entitled to the relief
claimed under Section 482 of BNSS.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside
the  order  passed  by  the  High  Court  dated
05.02.2026. 
We direct that in the event of arrest of the
appellant, the Arresting Officer shall release the
appellant  on  bail  subject  to  furnishing  cash
security in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-
Five Thousand only) with two like sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation
and trial, if any. 
3

## Page 139

The appellant shall not misuse her liberty and
shall not in any way influence the witnesses or
tamper with the material on record.
With  the  aforesaid  directions,  the  criminal
appeal is allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.11959/2026
[Arising out of SLP (C) No.27315/2026]
 
SURESH KUMAR & ORS.                      APPELLANTS
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.             RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appeal is directed against an order dated 16 th July, 2026
passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature for
Rajasthan at Jodhpur 1. Such order vacates an earlier order dated
29th January, 2026 granting interim relief in the writ appeal2 carried
by the appellant no.1 from the judgment and order dated 18 th
December, 2025, whereby a Single Judge of the High Court
dismissed their writ petition3.
3. We have noted that the Division Bench of the High Court had
granted interim relief on 29 th January, 2026 recording certain
reasons and also granted liberty to the Divisional Commissioner to
enquire and prepare a report in terms of Section 16 of the Right to
Fair  Compensation  and  Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,
1 High Court
2 D.B. Special Appeal Writ No.130/2026
3 S.B. Civil Writ Petition No.17703/2025
1

## Page 148

Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
4. However, while vacating the interim order dated 29 th January,
2026 vide the impugned order dated 16 th July, 2026, the Division
Bench did not advert to any change of circumstances since 29 th
January, 2026, which would warrant immediate vacation thereof.
The only reason assigned is that the interest of the defence
establishment should not be hampered. We have observed that the
situation prevailing on 29 th January, 2026 was much the same,
when interim relief was granted. The interim order having
continued for almost six months, without any further material being
brought on record justifying its vacation, the course adopted should
have been avoided.
5. In any event, since all the parties had entered appearance,
and if the matter could brook no further delay, it would have been
expedient in the interest of justice for the Division Bench to decide
the intra-court appeal one way or the other finally, instead of
vacating the earlier interim order. It is on this short ground that we
propose to interfere. 
6. The appeal stands disposed of, setting aside part of the
impugned order vacating interim relief granted earlier, with a
special request to the Division Bench of the High Court to attach
top priority to the intra-court appeal and to decide the same, as
expeditiously as possible and subject to its convenience, preferably
within a month from date of communication of this order. 
7. This special request is made to the Division Bench of the High
2

## Page 149

Court having regard to the fact that national security, which is of
paramount importance, is one of the serious concerns present in
this case. We record the assurance of the parties before us that
they shall extend full cooperation to the Division Bench to facilitate
early disposal of the appeal and not seek adjournment on any date.
8. Till such time the appeal is disposed of finally by the Division
Bench, the interim order dated 29th January, 2026 shall continue.
9. All points and contentions on merits are left open to be urged
by the parties before the Division Bench.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of. 
………………………………………J.
 [DIPANKAR DATTA]

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 12037/2026
(@ SLP (C) No.28736/2026)
DHARAM SINGH           APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.             RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  Civil  Appeal  (arising  out  of  Special  Leave
Petition) arises from the order dated 29.06.2026 in D.B.
Special Appeal Writ No. 423/2026.
4. The appeal is pending before the Division Bench of
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur.
5. The appeal is admitted and, as an interim measure,
the order impugned has been passed by the Division Bench.
The learned counsel appearing for the appellant contends
that granting an interim stay is one of the procedures
followed by Division Bench with a view to preventing the
successful party from executing the order under challenge
in the appeal but issuing a direction though couched in a
liberal expression virtually amounts to allowing the writ

## Page 163

2
appeal and circumstances would become  Fait  Accompli .
Therefore, while not objecting to granting the interim
stay  of  the  learned  Single  Judge’s  Judgment  dated
12.03.2026, emphasis is laid to the last sentence in the
order impugned.
6. Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned senior counsel for the
appellant contends that this sentence is read out of
context,  and  the  consideration  of  totality  of
circumstances  would  convince  this  Court  that  the
direction has been issued in the larger interest of the
villagers, including his client who has a valid mining
lease in his favour.
7. We have taken note of the submissions and perused
the record.
8. Having perused the order dated 12.03.2026 of the
learned Single Judge, we are of the view that the last
sentence in the order impugned is rendering the pending
writ appeal Fait  Accompli. Therefore, the last sentence
in the impugned order to wit “The appellant would be free
to  construct  the  culvert  over  the  water  body  and  take
care that the flow of the water body remains continuous”,
needs interference and is set aside.
9. The parties are given liberty to request the High
Court for early hearing and we have no doubt that the
High Court would do the needful.

## Page 164

3
10. The Civil Appeal is disposed of in above terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High
Court,  vide the  impugned  judgment  dated  09.12.2025,
dismissed the writ petition, holding that notice had been
duly served upon the appellant at its declared registered-
office  address  and  that,  despite  being  afforded  an
opportunity of hearing, the appellant had failed to appear.
4. The material placed before us, however, indicates that
the appellant-Company had changed its registered office in
the year 1996, whereas the notices issued by respondent No.
2 were addressed to its former address. Respondent No. 3 had
also corresponded with the appellant at its changed address
prior  to  the  initiation  of  the  deemed-conveyance
proceedings. Moreover, the public notice subsequently issued
neither  named  the  appellant  nor  contained  particulars
sufficient to identify the subject property.
5. Having regard to the nature and consequences of the
proceedings, we are satisfied that the appellant was not
afforded an adequate and effective opportunity of hearing
before  the  order-cum-certificate  dated  09.10.2013  was
passed.
6. For the reasons aforesaid, and solely on the limited
ground of violation of the principles of natural justice,
the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated
09.12.2025 passed by the High Court, as well as the order-
2

## Page 179

cum-certificate dated 09.10.2013 passed by respondent No. 2,
are hereby set aside.
7. The application filed by respondent No. 3-Society for
the grant of deemed conveyance is restored to the file of
respondent No. 2 for consideration afresh. The appellant-
Company shall file its objections, along with the material
upon which it seeks to rely, within four weeks from today.
Since the parties are represented before us, no fresh notice
need be issued to the appellant. Upon receipt of the
objections, respondent No. 2 shall afford the parties a
reasonable opportunity of hearing and pass a reasoned order
in  accordance  with  law.  The  entire  exercise  shall  be
concluded within three months from today.
8. Until the application is decided afresh, the parties
shall maintain status quo in respect of the subject land and
buildings and shall neither create any third-party rights
therein  nor  undertake  any  redevelopment  thereof.  This
direction shall not prevent respondent No. 3-Society from
carrying out routine maintenance and essential repairs in
respect of Buildings B and C.
9. It is clarified that the findings recorded by the High
Court in the impugned judgment shall not influence the fresh
determination by respondent No.2. The application shall be
considered independently, on the basis of the material
placed by the parties, and decided on its own merits and in
accordance with law.
3

10. We further clarify that this Court has not expressed
any opinion on the merits of the rival claims.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   4070   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 5197 OF 2026)
SHAILENDRA RAGHUWANSHI      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard Mr. Ajay Mishra, learned Senior
counsel  for  the  appellant;  Mr.  Rudraditya  Khare,
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh; and Mr. Abhishek Vikas, learned counsel for
Respondent No.2.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
03.09.2025 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh
at Jabalpur (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter),
rejecting  the  regular  bail  application  of  the
appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.225/2023
registered  at  Police  Station-  Udaipura,  District-
Raisen, Madhya Pradesh under Sections 302, 307, 353,
1

## Page 193

332, 294, 323, 147, 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) and Sections 25 and 27 of
the Arms Act, 1959.
5. This Court vide order dated 19.03.2026 had issued
notice  pursuant  to  which  respondent(s)  have  filed
counter-affidavit(s).
6.  Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  that  on
13.06.2023 at around 05:00 PM, 05 officials of the
village had gone to the shop of the appellant and
others  for  encroachment  measurement  as  there  were
allegations that their shops were encroaching public
land and drainage. This led to scuffle between the
appellant and other shopkeepers, on the one hand, and
officials and some other people, on the other hand. In
the violence that ensued, two of the other persons, who
suffered gunshot injuries allegedly fired by two of the
co-accused, died on way to the hospital.
7. Appellant was arrested on 17.06.2023 and is in
custody since then.
8. In  the  proceedings  held  on  12.08.2026,  the
following order came to be passed:
“2. In  terms  of  our  order  dated
05.08.2026, State of Madhya Pradesh has
filed an additional affidavit placing on
record that as of now, 14 prosecution
witnesses have been examined. The details
of the prosecution witnesses who have
2

## Page 194

been examined are mentioned in paragraph
4. It is stated in paragraph 5 that a
total of 20 more prosecution witnesses
are left to be examined out of whom 5 are
eye-witnesses. It is submitted that the
next  date  fixed  for  examination  of
prosecution witnesses is 21.08.2026 and
22.08.2026.
3. We direct that in these two days, the
evidence of the remaining eye-witnesses
may be recorded.
4. List on 25.08.2026, on which date we
may consider passing appropriate order.”
9. Today, learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Madhya Pradesh submits that 02 of the 05 prosecution
witnesses  stated  to  be  eye-witnesses  have  been
examined. Next date fixed is 08.09.2026 for examination
of the other eye-witnesses.
10. We  have  perused  the  materials  on  record  and
considered the submissions made by learned counsel for
both the sides.
11. Since the trial is in progress, without expressing
any  opinion  on  the  merits  of  the  accusations  but
considering the period of incarceration undergone by
the appellant which is more than 03 years, we are
inclined to grant bail to the appellant.
12. Having regard  to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 03.09.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
3

## Page 195

produced  before  the  jurisdictional  Sessions  Court
within  a  maximum  period  of  07  days  from  today,

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION   (Civil) NO.3393/2025
AISHWARYA GANGURI PETITIONER
VERSUS
RAHUL CHOWDARY KATRAGADDA RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Read the office report dated 24th August, 2026.
2. This  transfer  petition,  under  Section  25  of  the  Code  of  Civil
Procedure,  1908,  has  been  presented  by  the  petitioner-wife,
Aishwarya Ganguri.
3. The  marriage  between  the  petitioner  and  the  respondent-
husband,  Rahul  Chowdary  Katragadda,  was  solemnized  on  23 rd
February, 2023. One male child was  born to the petitioner and the
respondent from the wedlock on 13 th February, 2024.  However, the
parties have since drifted apart owing to differences arising by and
between them.
4. The respondent has instituted proceedings under Section 13(1)
(i-a) and (iii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 titled “ Rahul Chowdary
Katragadda  Vs.  Dr.  Aishwarya  Ganguri ” in  the  Family  Court,
Integrated Family Courts at Hyderabad, T elengana.
1

## Page 198

5. On the multiple grounds urged in the petition, the petitioner has
sought  for  transfer  of  the  aforesaid  proceedings  to  a  court  of
competent jurisdiction at Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
7. We  are  satisfied,  having  regard  to  the  inconvenience  the
petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were continued before
the Family Court at Hyderabad,  which is at a distance of around 650
kms  from  her  present  place  of  residence, that  interest  of  justice
demands grant of the prayer for transfer. 
8. Hence, the transfer petition is allowed. O. P . No.1250 of 2025
titled  “ Rahul  Chowdary  Katragadda  Vs.  Dr.  Aishwarya  Ganguri ”
pending  before  the  Family  Court,  Integrated  Family  Courts  at
Hyderabad is transferred to the Family Court/ Visakhapatnam District
Court  at  Visakhapatnam,  Andhra  Pradesh,  as  the  case  may  be,
having jurisdiction to hear the petition . Records of O. P . No.1250 of
2025 be transferred to the transferee court immediately .
9. T o avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 28 th September, 2026. If any or both the parties
fail to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee
court will fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free
to proceed in accordance with law.
10. Notwithstanding that mediation has failed, the presiding officer
of the transferee court shall endeavour to bring about a settlement
between the parties through the process of mediation. If the process
is unsuccessful, nothing shall preclude the presiding officer to take
2

## Page 199

the  proceedings  to  its  logical  conclusion  on  its  merits  and  in
accordance with law.
11. If the respondent is unable to attend the proceedings in person
on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to attend
through the virtual mode and if such a permission is sought, the
presiding officer of the court may proceed to consider it reasonably .
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

No.35/2020 and No.42/2020, affirming the conviction of

Instruments Act, 1881 in proceedings arising from C.C.
Nos.911/2005, 828/2005 and 874/2005.
2. The parties have arrived at a settlement in each of the
three cases. The Settlement Agreements dated 24.07.2026
have been forwarded by the Chairman, TLSC, Davanagere.
The terms of the three settlements are extracted below:
R.P.No.31/2020 CC No.911/2005
“2. The terms of settlement are as under:
We have agreed to get settled the matter.
The compensation ordered was Rs.1,25,000/-
and the respondents have agreed to receive

Rs.38,000/-.  There is deposit of Rs.39,000/-

R.P.No.35/2020 CC No.828/2005
“The terms of settlement are as under:

R.P. No.42/2020 CC No.874/2005
“2.  The terms of settlement are as under:

That the compensation ordered was Rs.45,000/-

and the respondent has agreed to receive the

3. The  respondent(s)  who  are  the  complainant(s)  in
proceedings under Section 138 of the N.I. Act are present
in  the  office  of  Secretary  District  Legal  Services
Authority, Davanagere and have appeared through video
conferencing. They have stated that they have received
the payment and the balance payment which is in lying in
deposit with the Trial court and this Court is to be
released in favour of the respondent(s).  They have also
agreed  that  the  conviction  of  the  petitioner  be
compounded in terms of the settlement. 
4. As parties have agreed to compound the proceedings basis
a settlement, having regard to the provisions of Section
147 of the N.I. Act and the law laid down by this Court
in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H1; Raj Reddy Kallem
v. State of Haryana2; B. V. Seshaiah v. State of Telengana
and another 3 and Gian Chand Garg v. Harpal Singh and
another4 that offence punishable under Section 138 of the
N.I. Act is compoundable with the consent of the parties
at any stage even after conviction, these petitions are
1 (2010) 5 SCC 663
2 (2024) 8 SCC 588
3 (2023) 18 SCC 512
4 2025 SCC OnLine SC 2317

## Page 224

disposed of in terms of the settlement and the offence
punishable  under  Section  138  of  N.I.  Act  stands
compounded.  In  consequence,  the  conviction  of  the
petitioner  under  Section  138  is  set  aside.  The
compensation amount(s) lying in deposit in the Trial
Court as well as this Court along with accrued interest,
if any, shall be released in favour of the respondent(s).

O R D E R
The applications for impleadment are rejected.
Leave granted.
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the parties.
We have also perused the impugned order passed
by the High Court.
This  is  a  case  where  the  respondents  were
arrayed as accused for the offences punishable under
Sections 420 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860  in  FIR  No.  392/2024  registered  at  Police
Station  Jayanagar,  Sub-division  Jayanagara,
Bengaluru. The High Court, vide the impugned order,
has quashed the First Information Report. 
On a prima  facie  view, we are of the opinion
that the High Court ought not to have undertaken the
aforesaid exercise, especially when the final report
is yet to be filed.
In such view of the matter, we are not inclined

## Page 234

2
to go into the merits of the case. 
Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside with a direction to the investigating agency
to file the final report within a period of three
months from the date of receipt of a copy of this
order.
Liberty is granted to the parties to challenge
the said final report in the manner known to law. 
In the meantime, the investigating agency shall
not arrest the respondents or take any coercive
steps against them, subject to their cooperation
with the investigation. 
Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, and the appeal is allowed.
We make it clear that we have not expressed
anything on the merits of the case. All issues are
left open.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Date : 24-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI

For Petitioner(s) : Ms. Ruchi Kohli, Sr. Adv.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The instant writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
has been filed in public interest, seeking Court-monitored forensic
audit and safeguards against unauthorized private access to the
data used for employment verification by the Employees’ Provident
Fund Organisation (EPFO) or for the Income Tax Return (ITR).
3. The  Petitioner  has  averred  that  an  unregulated,  private
employment verification ecosystem has emerged, wherein private
entities secure access, retrieve, and commercially use sensitive
1

## Page 246

employment and financial data. The said data corresponds to the
records maintained by the Income Tax Department and the Central
Board of Direct Taxes.
4. The Petitioner has referred to further material came to light
in April and May 2026, indicating a broader private verification
ecosystem.  This  material  includes  correspondence  with  private
entities, including Appexigo Technologies, describing data-fetching
and verification capability. In sum and substance, the Petitioner’s
case is that these entities are illegally and unauthorisedly
misusing the private data of these individuals. Such sensitive
statutory data is, thus, being accessed outside the protected
governmental ecosystem. It is also alleged that the data collected
at several functions is being repurposed for private commercial
streaming.
5. Such unauthorised access is said to be violative of Article 21
of the Constitution. Consequently, the Petitioner has sought, inter
alia, the following directions:
“a.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing  Respondent  Nos.1  to  8  and  all  concerned
authorities  to  immediately  take  preventive  and
protective measures to stop any further unlawful access,
dissemination,  disclosure,  transfer,  processing  or
misuse of EPFO/UAN-linked employment data, PAN-linked
information, ITR/Form 26AS/AIS-linked financial data and
other statutorily protected personal data;
b.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing Respondent Nos.1, 2, 6 and 7, in coordination
with  competent  agencies,  to  conduct  a  time-bound
independent technical / cyber-forensic inquiry into the
manner in which such statutory data is being accessed,
retrieved, processed or used within private verification
ecosystems;
c.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing Respondent Nos.3, 4 and 5 to disclose the
2

## Page 247

existing legal and technical safeguards, authentication
architecture,  API  controls  and  access-governance
mechanisms protecting statutory employment and financial
data,  and  to  clarify  whether  any  lawful  framework
permits the impugned access;
d.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing  Respondent  Nos.  1  to  8  to  identify  and
investigate  all  private  entities,  intermediaries,
processors,  API  providers,  ERJs,  aggregators,  user
applications,  third-party  applications,  and  other
connected  actors  involved  in  accessing,  processing,
storing,  transferring  or  commercially  using  such
statutory data under the guise of an integrated digital
consent framework;
e.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing Respondent Nos. 1, 2, 6 and 8 to frame and
notify'  appropriate  guidelines/safeguards  governing
digital  employment  verification,  background  screening
and access to statutory employment and financial data,
consistent with constitutional principles of privacy and
data  protection,  and  to  ensure  that  any  access,
processing or sharing of such data is undertaken only
through a lawful, transparent and accountable mechanism
based on free, informed and specific consent; 
f.  Issue  an  appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction
directing  competent  agencies  to  initiate  appropriate
action in accordance with law against persons/entities
found involved in unlawful access, misuse, unauthorized
disclosure or commercial exploitation of such data;
g. Pass such other and further order(s) as this Hon'ble
Court may deem fit and proper.”
6. In this regard, we find that the Petitioner has submitted a
comprehensive representation dated 21.03.2026 and 22.04.2026 to the
official Respondents, copies whereof have also been placed on
record. Since the issue involves a policy intervention, which must
take place on the recommendations of an Expert body, we dispose of
the writ petition, at this stage, with a direction to the Union of
India and other official Respondents to consider the representation
submitted by the Petitioner. Further, these Respondents are also
3

## Page 248

directed to take necessary action as may be required to prevent
misuse of the data maintained by Income Tax Department and Central
Board of Direct Taxes in the EPFO Passbook API and Form 26-AS API
and take such necessary measures as may be required to ensure that
such data is not misused by unauthorised private entities. It will
be  appreciated  if  a  comprehensive  decision  is  taken  and
communicated to the Petitioner, preferably within a period of four
months.
7. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
8. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                                   (NIKITA SINGH)

2. The issue pertains to effective representation of the women
members of the Bar in the composition of the Governing Bodies of
the Delhi High Court Bar Association and the Coordination Committee
of all the District Court Bar Associations/Coordinate Committee in
the upcoming elections in 2027.
3. Learned counsel, representing the Coordination Committee of
all the District Courts, graciously submitted that the Coordination
Committee is inclined to consider the issue at their own level, in
consultation with the Delhi High Court Bar Association and other
Bar Associations, for which four weeks’ time is granted.
4. We have no reason to doubt that the Coordination Committee
will come out with a solution that is acceptable to all and which

so that repeated orders for the same are not required to be passed
by this Court.

2 IT Act
1

## Page 288

2. In terms of an order of this Court, a Special Investigating Team 3 has been
constituted, which is in the process of investigating the crime registered on the
complaint of the private respondent.
3. By our order dated 20 th July, 2026, we have required the SIT to place the
final report in a sealed cover before us prior to the next date of hearing.
4. During pendency of the special leave petition, the SIT has registered a
fresh case, i.e., CID CB Cyber Crime PS Case No.15/2026 under Sections 318(2),
319(2), 336(2), 340(2) of the BNS, read with Sections 66-C and 66-D of the IT
Act against one Manas Kumar Mahapatra and other accused. Manas Kumar
Mahapatra has been arrested on 27th May, 2026. 
5. Learned counsel appearing for the State submits that upon completion of
investigation of CID CB Cyber Crime PS Case No.15/2026, charge-sheet under
Section 193 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 has filed before
the trial magistrate on 24 th August, 2026 in a sealed cover. However, since the
contents thereof would have some bearing on the final report that is proposed
to be filed in connection with Angul Town Police Station Case No.326/2025,
prayer is made so that the charge-sheet that has since been filed is not made
over to the accused therein, since that could hamper the investigation in CID CB
Cyber Crime PS Case No.15/2026. 
6. It is also submitted that since Manas Kumar Mahapatra has been in
custody for almost three months, it is likely that he could apply for bail.
7. Having regard to the apprehension expressed on behalf of the State, we
observe that since investigation of Angul Town Police Station Case No.326/2025
is still incomplete, the charge-sheet so filed in CID CB Cyber Crime PS Case
No.15/2026 may be looked into by the trial magistrate if Manas Kumar
3 SIT
2

## Page 289

Mahapatra applies for bail. If a case for grant of bail is made out, such bail may
be granted without, however, providing copies thereof to the accused in CID CB
Cyber Crime PS Case No.15/2026 at this stage. If, prima facie, no case for bail is
made out, the trial magistrate shall seek the leave of this Court for providing
copies of the charge-sheet to the accused before rejection of the prayer. In such
case, the said charge-sheet shall also be placed before us in a sealed cover.
8. The status report handed over today shall be retained in a sealed cover.
9. List the special leave petition on 25th September, 2026.
10. Interim protection from arrest granted to the petitioner by the previous
order dated 20th July, 2026 will continue till the next date of hearing.

                             O R D E R
1. The matter was taken up today for further hearing in the
Committee Room. The parties are personally present with their
children, Kiyan and Ishika. The learned counsel appearing for the
parties are also present. We heard one and all concerned.
2. We had met the parties last on May 6, 2026. 
3. By our Order dated May 6, 2026, we had suggested that the
parties should go for counseling to improve relationship between
them. We had also impressed upon the parties to go for counseling
with a positive mindset and not just for the sake of going for
counseling. In other words, we had impressed upon the parties that
the entire exercise should not be an empty formality. 
4. We are informed that paying heed of our suggestion, the
parties went before a Counselor by name Ms. James Ruth. Ms. James
Ruth is running a Center in the name of “Spring Health”. The
parties had around six sittings. After talking to the parties
individually, it appears that there has not been much progress
insofar as counseling with Ms. Ruth is concerned, although Ms. Ruth
might have tried her best to hel the parties.
5. We want the arrangement provided by us vide our Order dated
6-5-2026 to continue for some more time. However, today we have
been able to convince both Punit and Priya that they should go for
a fresh round of counseling but this time with Mr. Alok Mahapatra,
one of the well-renowned counselors in the city. The parties shall
seek an appointment with Mr. Mahapatra and start counseling at the
earliest. We request Mr. Mahapatra to try his best to help the
parties in all respects, more particularly, keeping in mind that
they have two minor children, Ishika  and Kiyan. 
6. Whatever may be the ultimate outcome of the counselling
process, we humbly request Mr. Mahapatra to provide us with one
report in a sealed cover in the last.
7. If Mr. Mahapatra wants some more time, he may make a request
by forwarding us a short report as regards the development that
have taken place till that point of time. 
8. The timings which we have provided are flexible. It is just a

## Page 313

3
matter of understanding.
9. These are all small issues but problem to crop up only from
small issues. Therefore, let both Punit and Priya proceed further
keeping in mind the welfare of their two minor children.
10. We have also persuaded Priya to give sufficient time to Punit
with the two children.
11. If Punit as a father would like to take his children out to a
mall or some park, picnic spots etc., Priya should be gracious
enough to allow Punit to take and she is always welcome to
accompany Punit. At a given time, if Kiyan wants to sleep with his
father, there should not be any problem in that regard.
12. We believe that this marriage can still be saved with little
understanding on the part of the parties. However, what seems to be
lacking is mutual respect for each other and trust. Without mutual
respect for each other and trust, no marriage can survive. 
13. From day one, we have been persuading the parties to just keep
one thing in mind i.e. their two minor children. All that we want
to convey to both Punit and Priya is that their conduct in public
should be such that none of the other should feel humiliated. 
14. We hope and trust that this fresh round of counseling may
help the parties in trying to understand each other and resolve
their misunderstanding.
15. Post this matter for further hearing on November 27, 2026. We
shall take up this matter in the second session in the Committee
Room.

Rules, 2016 (herein after referred to as “2016 Rules”) to
contend that the suspension order as passed against the
petitioner cannot sustain as the Competent Authority has not
taken a decision within the time stipulated under the said
Rule.  He on this basis contends that although the charge
sheet is being issued as per the instructions received by

2026, the suspension order should be revoked in the light of
the said Rule 5.
3. Having considered the submissions made by the learned
counsel for the petitioner with reference to Rule 5 of the
2016 Rules, we are not inclined to accept the said prayer as
made by the learned counsel for the petitioner as we  find
that there is a provision for the extension of time before
the time specified to comply with the requirement thereof,
subject to the exceptions as laid out therein.
4. We are not inclined to go into the reasons and whether
it would fulfill the requirement provided therein in the
light of the following reason.

moved an application for extension of time to comply with the
undertaking given to the Court which is coming up for
hearing, liberty is granted to the petitioner to press her

A W A R D
1. These petitions seek leave to impugn orders dated 18.07.2024
and 09.09.2024 by which the High Court set aside the Trial
Court’s Order acquitting the petitioner and convicted the
petitioner under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments
Act, 1881.
2. During pendency of these petitions, the parties have entered a
settlement  on  25.05.2026  in  the  presence  of  Secretary,
District Legal Services Authority, Kangra at Dharamshala.  The
District Legal Service Authority has forwarded the settlement
1

## Page 336

agreement which has been duly signed by the parties.
3. As per the settlement agreement, the petitioner has offered
Rs.5,40,000/- (Rupees Five Lakh Forty Thousand Only) along
with interest towards full and final settlement of the amount
payable to the respondent.
4. The terms of settlement are recorded in paragraph 2 of the
Settlement Agreement, which is extracted below:
“The present matter has been identified by the Hon'
ble Supreme court of India to be taken up in Special
Lok Adalat. The matter has been referred to the
mediator by the Secretary District Legal Services
Authority Kangra at Dharamshala on 23.05.2026. As
per the directions the parties appeared in the ADR
Center on 25.05.2026 and after various discussions
the parties entered to settle their dispute as
follows -
a. That the petitioner has been convicted by
the  Hon'ble  High  Court  Shimla  vide  its
judgment  dated  18.07.2024,  passed  in  Cr.
Appeal 130/2011.
b. That the petitioner has deposited the
whole  of  compensation  amount  i.e.
Rs.5,40,000/-  before  the  Additional  Chief
judicial Magistrate Kangra (H.P) Vide draft
number  "473519"  on  24.09.2024  issued  by
Punjab National Bank Kangra.
c.  That  the  petitioner  offered  to  the
respondent  that  the  respondent  will  get
release  the  said  amount  of  Rs.5.40,000/-
along with interest for which a second party
i.e.  Respondent  fully  satisfied  with  the
amicable settlement and left with no claim
against the petitioner.
d. That now there is nothing due payable by
the first party / petitioner to the second
party/respondent.
e. That the second party has no objection in
case the order passed by the Hon'ble High
Court Shimla passed in Cr. Appeal Number
130/2011 order dated 18.07.2024 be set aside
and the petitioner/ convict is acquitted in
2

## Page 337

the offence under section 138 of Negotiable
Instrument Act and the offence May kindly be
treated as compounded.”
5. As parties have agreed to compound the offence basis a
settlement, having regard to the provisions of Section 147 of
the N.I. Act and the law laid down by this Court in Damodar S.
Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H 1; Raj Reddy Kallem v. State of
Haryana2; B. V. Seshaiah v. State of Telengana and another3 and
Gian Chand Garg v. Harpal Singh and another 4 that offence
punishable under Section 138 of the N.I. Act is compoundable
with the consent of the parties at any stage, even after
conviction, these Special Leave Petitions are disposed of in
terms of the settlement. The offence punishable under Section
138 of N.I. Act shall stand compounded. The order of High
Court stands set aside accordingly.  The respondent, in terms
of the settlement, shall be entitled to withdraw the amount
lying in deposit (supra) along with interest, if not withdrawn
already.    
6. The settlement shall form part of the award.

A W A R D
1. This appeal arises from an order of the High Court of Delhi at
New Delhi dated 17.10.2023 passed in Criminal Revision Petition No.
875/2018, whereby the appellant’s revision petition against the
order  convicting  him  under  Section  138  of  the  Negotiable
Instruments Act, 1881 (“N.I. Act”) has been dismissed.
2. During the pendency of proceedings before the High Court, the
1

## Page 360

appellant had deposited Rs.2 lacs and before the Supreme Court
Rs.60,000 was deposited by the appellant.
3. Now the parties have arrived at a settlement in the Pre-
Special Lok Adalat Conciliation meeting held on 26.05.2026. The
terms  of  settlement  are  incorporated  in  paragraph  2  of  the
Settlement agreement dated 26.05.2026, which has been forwarded by
the  Secretary,  Delhi  Legal  Services  Authority,  East,  Delhi.
Paragraph 2 is extracted below:
“2. The terms of settlement are as under:-
(a) It is agreed between the parties that
they have settled their dispute for a sum
of Rs.2,60,000/- as the full and final
settlement  amount.
(b) It is agreed between the parties that
the  appellant/accused  Satya  Pal  Dhawan
shall pay a sum of Rs.2,60,000/-, by way
of Demand Draft, drawn in favour of the
respondent Anil Kumar, to be handed over
in  presence  of  Ld.  Counsels  for  the
parties  on  11.08.2026.
(c) It is agreed between the parties that
the appellant is at liberty to withdraw
the amount of Rs.2,60,000/- along with
interest up to date, if any, lying with
the registry of Hon'ble Supreme Court.
(d) It is agreed between the parties that
after  receiving  the  full  and  final
settlement  amount,  the  respondent  Anil
Kumar  will  give/issue  No  Objection
Certificate in favour of the appellant for
release of the amount of Rs.2,60,000/-
along with interest, if any, up to date.”
2

## Page 361

4. In terms of the settlement, the appellant-accused was required
to pay a Sum of Rs. 2,60,000/- by way of Demand Draft to the
Respondent- Anil Kumar, who is present in person. Anil Kumar states
that he has been handed over a demand draft of Rs. 2,60,000/-.
5. Having regard to the provisions of Section 147 of the N.I. Act
and the law laid down in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H 1; Raj
Reddy Kallem v. State of Haryana 2; B. V. Seshaiah v. State of
Telengana and another 3 and Gian Chand Garg v. Harpal Singh and
another4 that an offence punishable under Section 138 of the N.I.
Act is compoundable with the consent of the parties at any stage
even after conviction,  let an award be drawn in terms of the
settlement. In consequence,  the conviction is set aside, the
offence punishable under Section 138 of the N.I. Act shall stand
compounded. The amount of Rs.2 lacs deposited before the High Court
and Rs.60,000 which has been deposited before this Court along with
accrued interest, if any, shall be released in favour of the
appellant in terms of the settlement. The settlement shall be part
of the award.

no. 4.
2. It is informed that during the pendency of these proceedings,
respondent nos. 1 and 3 have passed away and respondent no. 2 is
the sole surviving legal heir who has been duly substituted to
represent the estate of respondent nos. 1 and 3.  The respondent
nos.  1  and  3  had  challenged  the  auction  sale  conducted  by
respondent  no.  4  in  which  the  petitioners  were  the  auction
purchasers.

## Page 414

3. By the impugned order dated 05.01.2018, auction sale was set
aside and respondent nos. 1-3 were directed to deposit the entire
auction sale amount with interest from the date of auction till the
date of the order before the executing firm.
4. During pendency of these proceedings, parties have entered
into a settlement. The auction purchaser is giving up his rights in
the subject property and is acceding to the judgment passed by the
High Court, subject to the respondent no. 2 paying a sum of Rs.
12,50,000/- to the auction purchasers.  It is agreed that out of
the said amount of Rs. 12,50,000/-, a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 has
already been paid to the auction purchasers.
5. Further, it is agreed that the sum of 5,79,000/-, which has
been deposited with the executing Court along with any interest
accrued thereon, be released in favour of the auction purchasers,
i.e. in favour of the petitioners herein.
6. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  respondent  no.  2,  under
instructions  from  respondent  no.  2,  undertakes  on  behalf  of
respondent no. 2 that respondent no. 2 shall pay the balance agreed
amount of Rs. 5,71,000/- to the petitioners within a period of two
weeks from today.  Said undertaking is accepted.
7. In view of the above, the final settlement report dated
21.08.2026 is taken on record.  This Court has perused the terms of
settlement and finds the same to be lawful.  Parties shall be bound
by the terms of the settlement.  In view of the undertaking given
by respondent no. 2 and release of the amount, learned counsel for
the petitioner seeks leave to withdraw the petition.
8. The executing Court is directed to release the entire amount
deposited with the executing Court along with interest accrued
thereon to the petitioners.  Further, the executing Court shall
issue a certificate entitling respondent no. 2 (original petitioner
before the High Court) to refund of the amount of the stamp duty as
directed by the impugned order, in paragraph 38(e).

case, it will not warrant disqualification under Section
36 of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1958.
3. The  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
respondents submits that the findings of the District
Collector has been rightly considered by the High Court,
which shows that the convening of the meetings itself is
in doubt.
4. Considering that the aforesaid finding, as submitted
by  the  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
respondents,  is  a  factual  finding,  the  resultant
conclusion would be that the mandatory meetings in a
Financial Year have not been conducted by the petitioner.
In such an eventuality, the rigor of Section 36 of the
Maharashtra  Village  Panchayats  Act,  1958,  has  been
rightly applied to the case of the petitioner.
5. In such view of the matter, we are not inclined to
interfere with the impugned order passed by the High
Court.  Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition stands
dismissed.

2. The petitioner has instituted the present proceedings

Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1972 also does not hold any
position, as the challenge has been made after nearly a
decade.   It  is  a  case  of  continuous  default  as
acknowledged by the petitioner’s mother herself in the
deposition dated 17.09.2007.  The possession of the
allotted plot has been taken away long time back, which
has now been allotted to a third party.
4. Accordingly, we find no reason to interfere with the
impugned order passed by the High Court.
5. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, dismissed
in the above terms.

of 6% per annum. However, we make it clear that the said amount shall be kept
in a Fixed Deposit and it is needless to state that successful party would be
entitled to receive the amount so deposited with accrued interest thereon if
any.

1

Court  wherein  the  order  of  the  Tribunal  was
challenged by other persons. It appears that the
writ petition of those other persons was dismissed
by the High Court against which they have filed
Special Leave Petition before this Court, which is
pending as SLP (C) Diary No. 22653/2026.
2. In such circumstances, the appropriate course
for the petitioner(s) is to move an intervention
application in the pending Special Leave Petition
rather than to file separate Special Leave Petition
against the order of the High Court which stands in
their favour.
3. Permission to file Special Leave Petition is,
accordingly, rejected.
4. The  Special  Leave  Petition  is,  therefore,
dismissed as not maintainable at the behest of the
petitioner(s).
5. However, the petitioner(s) shall have liberty to
file intervention application in the pending SLP (C)
Diary No. 22653/2026.

252506/2026 shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The submission of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that Trial Court’s decree decided the
issue of possession in favour of the petitioner and,
therefore, decreed the suit for injunction and not
for the alternative relief of possession. Therefore,
there was no occasion for him to challenge the
decree passed by the Trial Court by way of cross
appeal. However, the First Appellate Court held the
issue  of  possession  against  the  petitioner  but
granted the alternative relief of possession upon
1

## Page 538

finding that the petitioner was the owner. Such
power vested in the Appellate Court under Order 41
Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. In
such circumstances, the High Court was not justified
in setting aside the Trial Court decree on the
ground  that  there  was  no  cross  appeal  by  the
petitioner,  therefore  the  decree  for  possession
could not have been granted. 
2. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.

biological mother (first respondent).

A W A R D
1. These Special Leave Petitions arise from judgment and order of
the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla dated 18.07.2024,
whereby  the  High  Court  reversed  the  order  of  acquittal  and
convicted the petitioner under Section 138 of the Negotiable
Instruments Act, 1881 (“N.I. Act”).
2. During pendency of these proceedings, the parties have arrived
at a settlement where under the petitioner has paid total sum of
Rs. 5 lacs to the respondent. One lac was paid earlier and Rs.4
lacs have been paid vide demand draft No.001406 dated 09.10.2024
drawn on HDFC Bank, Baijnath.

## Page 710

3. The petitioner has prayed that the petition be allowed in
terms  of  the  settlement  as  the  respondent  has  agreed  for
compounding and no further amount is required to be paid to the
respondent.
4. Having regard to the provisions of Section 147 of the N.I. Act
and the law laid down by this Court in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed
Babalal H1; Raj Reddy Kallem v. State of Haryana2; B. V. Seshaiah v.
State of Telengana and another3 and Gian Chand Garg v. Harpal Singh
and another4 that an offence punishable under Section 138 of the
N.I. Act is compoundable with the consent of the parties at any
stage, even after conviction, these Special Leave Petitions are
disposed of in terms of the settlement and the offence punishable
under Section 138 of the N.I. Act is hereby compounded and the
order of conviction is set aside. 
5. The settlement shall be part of the award.

                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF WEST BENGAL                           Respondent(s)
(IA No. 236772/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT)
 
Date : 31-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Mr. Farrukh Rasheed, AOR
                   Ms. Harshita Singhal, Adv.
                   Mr. Syed M Hurmul, Adv.
                   Mr. Ekram Ali, Adv.
                   Mr. Shakil Ahmed, Adv.                   
For Respondent(s) : 
                   Mr. Nishant Awana, AOR
                   Mr. G.S. Awana, Adv.
                   Mr. Suraj Kundu, Adv.
                   Mr. Amough Pandey, Adv.                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Exemption Application is allowed.
2. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
3. It appears on plain reading of the impugned Order that
the High Court had earlier directed the trial court to
complete the trial within a period of six months. To be
precise, the High Court had directed that at least six

## Page 758

2
witnesses including the seizure list witnesses should be
examined within a period of six months. 
4. When the impugned Order came to be passed, the High Court
noted that not a single witness had been examined although
charge had already been framed long time back. 
5. It is very unfortunate as noted by the High Court in its
impugned Order that there was no Presiding Officer from 2nd
January, 2026 to 24th June 2026, and in such circumstances the
trial did not proceed further. 
6. In view of the aforesaid, we are persuaded to exercise
our discretion insofar as grant of bail to the petitioner is
concerned.
7. The petitioner is, accordingly, ordered to be released
on bail, subject to the terms and conditions to be imposed by
the  Trial Court.
8. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
9. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)
